lessons.title: Welcome to Pyeduc!
lessons.description: A brief introduction on how to get the most out of this app.
lessons.content:
### Hello and Welcome to Pyeduc! 👋

We created this app to make your Python learning journey as practical and enjoyable as possible.

Here you will have your progress automatically saved. Each student has their own isolated environment.

How does **Pyeduc** work?
- **Theoretical Classes**: Short and direct texts, followed by a Quiz to test your knowledge.
- **Practical Classes**: You will have a real **Python Console** to type and run your codes.

Use the "Next" and "Previous" buttons in the footer to navigate through classes.
Don't be in a rush, study at your pace. Programming is an incredible tool!
tips: Use the gray divider bar between the explanation and the quiz to resize the screen in your favor!
Don't be afraid to make mistakes in quizzes. You can try as many times as you want.

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The History of Python
lessons.description: Find out who created Python and why it's so popular.
lessons.content:
The Python language was created by **Guido van Rossum** and officially launched in 1991.

Development of the project began in late 1989, but the first public version (**Python 0.9.0**) was made available in February 1991 on the alt.sources discussion forum.

**The Origin of the Name:**
Contrary to what many think, the name **Python** has no relation to the reptile (python). In fact, during the creation of the language, Guido read the published scripts of the famous British comedy series **"Monty Python's Flying Circus"**. Needing a name that was short, unique and slightly mysterious for his project, he decided to name it Python!
tips: Python is an interpreted language, which means it doesn't need to be compiled before executing.
Python's philosophy (The Zen of Python) states that 'Readability counts'.

quiz.question: Who is the brilliant creator of the Python language?

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Why was Python created?
lessons.description: Understand Guido van Rossum's motivations and predecessor language.
lessons.content:
Guido van Rossum worked at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica in the Netherlands) on a project involving the **ABC** language.

The **ABC** language was very easy to teach to beginners but had severe limitations for more complex tasks. On the other hand, languages ​​like C were very hard to read.

Guido's goal in creating Python was to combine the best of both worlds: to create a language that was as **simple and readable as ABC**, but with the **power and features of C** to handle the operating system.

**The Great Differentiator:**
Python's number one priority has always been to be **easy to read, easy to learn, and easy to maintain**. Its clean code resembles plain English and gets rid of curly braces and semicolons. This makes reading and team collaboration infinitely faster compared to messy and structurally cluttered languages.
tips: Python's main goal has always been code clarity and readability.
Many concepts that make Python easy were directly inspired by ABC.

quiz.question: What language did Python succeed and draw heavily from?

lessons.title: Class 3: The Python Ecosystem
lessons.description: Discover where Python is used and learn about its giant ecosystem.
lessons.content:
One of Python's greatest strengths is its **Ecosystem**. The language has the philosophy of coming with "Batteries Included", that is, its **Standard Library** is gigantic and already comes with native tools to deal with the internet, files, advanced mathematics, databases (such as SQLite), and much more, without having to install anything extra.

Furthermore, Python supports practically **all platforms**: Windows, macOS, Linux, and even microcontrollers.

Thanks to this versatility, the community has developed incredible libraries that make Python dominate areas such as:
- **Web Development** (Django, Flask, FastAPI)
- **Data Analysis and Big Data** (Pandas, NumPy)
- **Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning** (TensorFlow, PyTorch)
- **Task Automation** (RPA, Scripts)
tips: The official repository for extra packages is called PyPI (Python Package Index).
You use the 'pip install' command to download these extra libraries created by the community.

quiz.question: In which of these areas is Python widely used? (Select all correct options)

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Compiled vs Interpreted
lessons.description: Discover the difference between compiled and interpreted languages.
lessons.content:
Have you ever stopped to think about how the computer understands the code we write?

There are two main approaches:

**1. Compiled Languages (Ex: C, C++)**
The entire code is translated (compiled) at once into machine language (binary) before being executed. It's like translating an entire book into another language before publishing it. This makes them very fast, but you have to compile again every time you make a change.

**2. Interpreted Languages (Ex: Python, JavaScript)**
The code is read and executed line by line by a program called **Interpreter**. It's like having a simultaneous translator listening and translating your speech in real time. This makes development much more agile and easier to test, as you don't need to compile the entire program for each change.

Python is classified as an interpreted language, which explains its incredible flexibility and development speed!
tips: Despite being interpreted, Python secretly translates the code to an intermediate format called Bytecode to gain speed.
Python's interpreted nature is what enables our Interactive Console (REPL) to work.

quiz.question: According to the text, what is the main characteristic of an interpreted language like Python?
options: It is transformed into binary all at once before running.
It is read and executed line by line by the Interpreter.
It only runs on Windows computers.
It does not need RAM memory to work.

lessons.title: Class 5: Source Code and .py Files
lessons.description: Understand what source code is and how we save our scripts in Python.
lessons.content:
For the computer to execute our instructions, we need to write them to a file. The set of all instructions written by us is called **Source Code**.

In Python, source code files use the **.py** extension at the end of their name. For example: **my_game.py** or **calculator.py**.

When you write Python code and save it with the **.py** extension, you are creating what we call a **Python Script**.

You can edit a **.py** file in absolutely any text editor (even Notepad!), but most programmers use specialized environments called **IDE** (like VS Code or PyCharm) that colorize words and help you find errors easily.
tips: The .py extension is what tells your operating system that this file should be opened using the Python interpreter.
Always use names without spaces for your Python files. Example: use 'my_script.py' instead of 'my script.py'.

quiz.question: What is the official extension used to save files containing the source code of a Python program?

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Python Versions (2 vs 3)
lessons.description: Discover the difference between Python versions and why staying up to date is essential.
lessons.content:
Like any technology, Python evolves over time. The biggest and most famous break in the history of the language occurred with the transition from **Python 2** to **Python 3**.

Released in 2008, Python 3 introduced such profound improvements to the way the language was processed and organized that it broke compatibility with older Python 2 code. This meant that code written for Python 2 often wouldn't work in Python 3 without being rewritten.

**Why Migrate?**
Although painful, the migration was essential! Python 3 brought dramatic performance improvements, universal native support for characters from all languages ​​(Unicode/UTF-8), and a much cleaner ecosystem. Python 2 was **officially retired and killed** in the year 2020. Using it today is a serious security risk.

Today we are already in versions like Python 3.12+, where the language becomes increasingly robust and faster with each annual update.
tips: Always start new projects using the latest version of Python 3.
If you find very old tutorials on the internet using 'print hello' without parentheses, know that it's from the defunct Python 2!

quiz.question: Why did the programming community decide to permanently abandon Python 2?
options: Because it started to be charged and stopped being free.
To force companies to buy new computers.
Because it has been officially retired, making it insecure and obsolete compared to Python 3.
Because its creator lost the source code in 2020.

lessons.title: Lesson 7: How to install Python?
lessons.description: Learn step-by-step how to install Python on Windows and Linux.
lessons.content:
To start programming on your own computer, you need to install the Python interpreter.

**On Windows:**
1. Go to the official website: python.org/downloads.
2. Download the latest installer.
3. **VERY IMPORTANT:** During installation, check the box **'Add Python to PATH'** on the first screen before clicking 'Install Now'. This ensures the terminal recognizes Python commands.

**On Linux (Ubuntu/Debian):**
Linux usually comes with Python pre-installed! To update it or make sure you have it, open the terminal and type:
`sudo apt update`
`sudo apt install python3 python3-pip`

That's it! To verify if the installation worked, simply open the terminal or command prompt and type `python --version` (on Windows) or `python3 --version` (on Linux).
tips: Don't forget 'Add Python to PATH' on Windows. If you miss it, you'll have to reinstall or configure it manually.
pip (included in the installation) is the package manager that lets you download new libraries in the future.

quiz.question: What is the most critical step when installing Python on Windows to ensure commands work in the terminal?
options: Check the 'Add Python to PATH' box
Install it on a flash drive

lessons.title: Lesson 8: What are IDEs and Code Editors?
lessons.description: Discover the tools programmers use to write code efficiently.
lessons.content:
An **IDE** (Integrated Development Environment) or a **Code Editor** is the program where you type your scripts. Think of it as the 'Microsoft Word' for programmers, but filled with tools that color your code, help find errors before running, and auto-complete words.

Can you write code in Notepad? Yes, but it will be very painful!

**Top Editors and IDEs in the Market:**
- **VS Code (Visual Studio Code)**: The most popular editor in the world. Very lightweight and expandable with extensions.
- **PyCharm**: An extremely powerful and robust IDE created specifically for Python, ideal for giant projects.
- **Jupyter Notebook**: Widely used in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence, as it allows mixing code, text, and visual graphs on the same screen.
- **IDLE**: The simple editor that comes pre-installed with Python.
tips: For beginners, VS Code is almost always the best starting point as it is fast and friendly.
IDEs have built-in terminals, meaning you can code and run the code on the same screen, just like this app!

quiz.question: Which IDE listed above was created specifically for the Python language and is focused on robust projects?

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Comments and Documentation
lessons.description: Learn to annotate your code to explain what it does.
lessons.content:
Comments are annotations you make in the code. Python completely ignores any text that comes after a hashtag (`#`). They are used to explain the code, leave warnings for other programmers, or even to temporarily 'disable' a piece of code you don't want to run.

You can also use three single (`'''`) or double (`"""`) quotes to create multi-line comments.
lessons.example:
# Printing a message
print('Hello!')  # This is an inline comment

lessons.title: Lesson 10: Rules for Naming Variables
lessons.description: Learn the snake_case pattern and how to name your variables correctly.
lessons.content:
Before we start creating variables and writing real code, we need to learn the Python baptism rules!

In programming, there are strict rules about what can and cannot be the name of a variable:
1. **No spaces**: You can never use spaces. **low price** will generate an error!
2. **Without accentuation or cedilla**: Forget correct Portuguese. Instead of **Greeting**, write **greeting**. Instead of **price**, use **price**.
3. **Don't start with numbers**: **1_place** will give an error, but **place_1** is accepted.

### The Snake Case Pattern 🐍
In Python, the community has adopted a pattern called **snake_case** (snake case). In it, we use lowercase letters and replace spaces with an _underline_ (**_**).

- ❌ Wrong: **low price**, **Lower Price** or **low price**
- ✅ Right: **low_price**

Adopting this standard from day one will make your code professional and readable to any programmer in the world!
tips: Lembre-se: O Python é 'Case Sensitive', ou seja, a variável 'Idade' (com I maiúsculo) é completamente diferente da variável 'idade' (com i minúsculo).
Tente sempre dar nomes que façam sentido. Variáveis como 'a' ou 'x' deixam o código confuso de ler.

lessons.title: Class 8: Variables and Texts (Strings)
lessons.description: Learn what a variable is and how to store text in it.
lessons.content:
Think of a **Variable** as a little box or label where you store data in the computer's memory to use later. To give this box a name, simply write the name and use the equals symbol **=**.

One of the most common data types is **Text** (called **String** in programming). To let Python know that you are writing free text and not a system command, you must **mandatoryly wrap the text in quotation marks** (single or double).

To show the value of this variable on the screen, we use the **print()** magic function.

**Dissecting the code below:**
- **=** ➔ Assignment sign (means "takes the value of").
- **name** ➔ Variable that will store the data.
- **"Alice"** ➔ Text (String) that will be stored. Mandatory with quotation marks!
- **print** ➔ Command used to show something on the screen.
- **(name)** ➔ We give the variable to print so it can show what's inside.

### Exploring Strings
You can use escape characters to format text:
- **\n**: Creates a new line (line break).
- **\t**: Creates a tab (long space).

If you don't want characters like \ to be interpreted (like in file paths), use **raw strings** by adding an **r** before the opening quotation marks.

You can also play with strings by doing math operations! You can use **+** to join (concatenate) and **\*** to repeat.
Two side-by-side string literals are automatically joined by Python. This is great for breaking long strings into multiple lines of code using parentheses.
lessons.example:
name = "Alice"
message = 'Hello, welcome!'

print(name)
print(message)

# New line and Tab
print('First line.\nSecond line.')
print('Name:\tAlice')

# Raw string (ignores escapes)
print(r'C:\some\folder')

# Concatenation and Repetition
print(3 * 'un' + 'ium')

# Joining literal strings and breaking long text
long_text = ('This is a very large text ' 
             'that was broken into two lines of code.')
print('Py' 'thon')
print(long_text)
tips: There can't be spaces in the variable name! Use an underscore '_' (snake_case) instead.
Remember: without quotes, Python will think your text is the name of a variable that doesn't exist!

socratic_hints: What happens if you try to print a variable without assigning a value to it first?
Did you check if your string is wrapped in single or double quotes?
Remember the equals sign '=': it is used to store the value in the variable.

### F-Strings (Formatted Texts)
One of the most modern and easiest ways to mix texts with variables is using **f-strings**. Just put the letter **f** before the initial quotation marks and wrap the variables in curly brackets **{}**. Python will automatically replace the keys with the variable value when printing!

**Example:**
```python

fruit = "apple"
print(f"I'm {age} years old and I like {fruit}.")
```

lessons.title: Class 9: Integers (Int)
lessons.description: See how to deal with exact math and integers.
lessons.content:
In addition to texts, variables are incredible for storing numbers! The most basic numeric type is **Integer** (called **int**).

Integers are positive or negative numbers that **do not have a decimal place**. 

The rule of thumb here is: **Don't use quotation marks for numbers!** If you put quotation marks around a number (e.g. **"10"**), Python will treat it as text and will not be able to do mathematical calculations with it.

**Dissecting the code below:**
- **age** ➔ The name of our variable.
- **=** ➔ The signal that stores the information in the variable.
- **25** ➔ The number itself, without using quotes! It is this true numeric value that will be stored in the variable called age.
- **print("Age:", age)** ➔ The print can show texts (with quotation marks) mixed with variables, just separate them with a comma.
lessons.example:
idade = 25
ano_nascimento = 1998
temperatura = -5

print("Idade:", idade)
print("Ano:", ano_nascimento)
print("Frio:", temperatura)
tips: Você pode somar variáveis de números usando o sinal de '+' diretamente no print.
O Python não tem limite de tamanho para números inteiros. Eles podem ser gigantescos!

lessons.title: Class 10: Decimal Numbers (Float)
lessons.description: Learn to record weights, heights and coins with broken numbers.
lessons.content:
For numbers that are not exact, such as money, measurements or weight, we use the **Decimal** type, known in programming as **Float**.

Pay attention to a crucial rule: Python was created using the American standard, so **we always use PERIOD (.) instead of a comma** to separate decimal places!

Writing **1.75** (with a comma) will break your code or create a Tuple (we'll see about this later). The correct option is to always use **1.75**.

**Dissecting the code below:**
- **height** ➔ The name chosen for the variable.
- **=** ➔ Command to assign the value.
- **1.75** ➔ Decimal Number (Float). Note the use of the DOT in place of the comma!
- **print("Height:", height)** ➔ Shows the guide text on the screen, followed by the broken number stored in memory.

lessons.title: Class 11: Boolean Values ​​(Bool)
lessons.description: Discover how the computer makes logical decisions (Yes or No).
lessons.content:
In the world of computing, everything boils down to false or true. We use the **Boolean** type (**bool**) to represent this duality.

A Boolean variable stores only two absolute values:
- **True**
- **False** (False)

**Warning:** They must begin with a CAPITAL letter in Python!

In addition to setting these values ​​directly, the computer can discover the truth by making **comparisons**! The result of a comparison will always be a Boolean (True or False). The most common symbols are:
- **>** (Greater than)
- **<** (Less than)
- **==** (Equals. Attention: we use two equals signs to test equality, not to be confused with the sign to create variables!)

**Dissecting the code below:**
- **jogo_pausado = False** ➔ We created the variable with the logical value.
- **10 > 5** ➔ The computer checks and returns **True** (true, 10 is greater than 5).
- **1 == 2** ➔ The computer checks and returns **False** (lie, 1 is not equal to 2).
lessons.example:
game_paused = False

print("Paused?", game_paused)
print("Logged in?", user_logged_in)

print("Is 1 equal to 2?", 1 == 2)
tips: Você nunca usa aspas para True ou False. Se usar aspas, vira um mero texto!
Eles serão a fundação para quando aprendermos sobre a estrutura de condição (IF).

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Arithmetic Operators
lessons.description: Basic Mathematical Operations in Python
lessons.content:
Just as we use calculators to do math, in programming we use **Arithmetic Operators**! They are the symbols responsible for carrying out all mathematical calculations within Python, from simple bakery bills to spatial equations.

Below you can see the main operators available in the language:

- **+** (addition): Adds two values.
- **-** (subtraction): Subtracts one value from another.
- **\*** (multiplication): Multiplies the values ​​(we use the asterisk!).
- **/** (division): Divides and always returns a broken number (decimal).
- **//** (integer division): Divides but cuts the decimal part, leaving only the integer.
- **%** (modulo): Takes only the **remainder** of the division (great for knowing if a number is even or odd).
- **\*\*** (exponentiation): Raises one number to the power of another (ex: 2 ** 3 is 8).
lessons.example:
years = 10
days_in_year = 365
a = 20

lessons.title: Lesson 16: Lists and Iteration
lessons.description: Work with lists and loops in Python
lessons.content:
Think of a list in Python as a box that holds several items at the same time.

**What is it for?**
- Save several data together in the same variable (like a shopping list: bread, milk, eggs).
- Access a specific item (the 1st, the 2nd…).
- Go through all the items one by one to do something (e.g. print each name).

**How it works in practice (very simple)**
In Python, you create a list like this:
```python
shopping = ["bread", "milk", "eggs"]
```
Now `shopping` is the “box” with 3 items.

**How to get an item**
You can take it by its “number” (index). **Attention:** in Python the count starts at 0.

- `shopping[0]` is the first item (“bread”)
- `shopping[1]` is the second (“milk”)
- `shopping[2]` is the third (“eggs”)

Example:
```python
print(purchases[1]) # will print: milk
```

**How to exchange an item (Replace)**
You can easily exchange what is inside a position by entering the index and a new value.
```python
Compras[1] = "chocolatado" # The 'milk' was replaced by chocolate!
```

**How to get around (see all)**
Generally you use `for` to do something with each item:
```python
for item in purchases:
    print(item)
```
This will print bread, then milk, then eggs.

**Want to add or take things away?**
Add at the end:
```python
purchases.append("banana")
```
Remove the last one (the end):
```python
shopping.pop()
```
lessons.example:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "orange"]

print("First fruit:", fruits[0])
# len() comes from 'length'. Counts how many items are in the box.
print("Number of fruits:", len(fruits))

print("\nAll fruits:")
# for = 'for each'. in = 'inside'. (For each fruit inside fruits:)
for fruit in fruits:
    print("-", fruit)

# You can also easily replace items!
fruits[0] = "strawberry"
print("\nWe replaced the apple with a strawberry:")
print(fruits)

# append() means to attach/add at the end.
fruits.append("watermelon")
print("\nAfter adding watermelon:")
print(fruits)
tips: List indices start at 0 and end at length - 1.
You can use negative indices, where -1 accesses the last element.

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Opening your Appetite
lessons.description: Find out why Python is the perfect tool for automating boring tasks.
lessons.content:
You know those repetitive tasks on the computer that make you lazy just thinking about? Python was created precisely to be your automation 'magic wand'! With it, you write small scripts that do the heavy lifting for you.

And the best part: Python is an **interpreted language**. This means you don't have to go through boring and time-consuming 'compiling' processes (translating everything into the machine) before testing. You write the code and it runs immediately. Just like that!
tips: In Python, you can save useful pieces of code (modules) and reuse them in other projects.
The language comes with 'batteries included': a gigantic library of ready-to-use tools.

lessons.content:
Imagine that **Interactive Mode** is like opening a WhatsApp chat directly with your Python brain! When you open the terminal and type `python3` you enter this chat room.

There, Python waits for your messages showing three arrows: `>>>`. Just type a mathematical or text command, press Enter, and it responds instantly! If you send a message that needs more than one line (like a condition), it shows three dots `...` to say: 'Go ahead, I hear you!'.
lessons.example:
>>> the_world_is_flat = True
>>> if the_world_is_flat:
...     print("Be careful not to fall off!")
...
Be careful not to fall off!
tips: To exit interactive mode on Unix/Linux, you can type Ctrl-D or the quit() command.
On Windows, you can exit by pressing Ctrl-Z followed by Enter.

lessons.title: Class 16: Passing Arguments
lessons.description: Understand how to send 'extra ingredients' to your program before it runs.
lessons.content:
Sometimes, your program needs external information right when it is turned on. Imagine that your script is a cake recipe, and you want to tell the flavor before 'Play' (ex: `python3 faz_bolo.py chocolate`).

These extra ingredients are called **Arguments**. Python takes everything you type after the program name and stores it in a special box called `sys.argv`. Item number zero (`sys.argv[0]`) is always the name of your file, and item number one (`sys.argv[1]`) is already the word 'chocolate'!
lessons.example:
# If we run in the terminal: python3 script.py argument1

print(sys.argv[0])  # Displays: 'script.py'
print(sys.argv[1])  # Displays: 'argumento1'
tips: To access the sys.argv list, you must import the sys module using 'import sys'.
If no script is passed (interactive mode), sys.argv[0] will be an empty string.

Have you ever opened a website and seen strange characters like 'Ã§Ã£o' instead of cedillas and accents? This happens when the computer misses the reading 'dictionary'.

To avoid this, Python defaults to a super dictionary called **UTF-8**. It is capable of understanding characters from practically every language in the world, including emojis! Thanks to UTF-8, you can write variables and comments with accents (ç, ã, é) without fear of breaking the program.

sections.content:
Python is an excellent calculator! To add, subtract and multiply we use the signs we already know (`+`, `-`, `*`). But division has a trick: the `/` operator always returns a 'broken' number (decimal with a comma, which in Python uses a period, called **float**).

If you want to split something ignoring the smaller chunks (integer splitting), use the double slash `//`. If you want to know what is 'left' after the division (the rest of the pizza), use the percentage symbol `%`. And to square or cube a number, we do not use the caret, but two asterisks `**`!
sections.example:
# Normal division (returns float)
print(17 / 3)   # 5.666666666666667

# Integer division (discards the fraction)
print(17 // 3)  # 5

# Remainder of division
print(17 % 3)   # 2

# Exponentiation (2 to the power of 7)
print(2 ** 7)   # 128

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Advanced Strings - Indexes and Slicing
lessons.description: Learn how to slice texts and get just the letters you want.
tips: Texts (strings) are immutable. You can't change a single letter of an already created text, you can only create a whole new text.
If you try to access a position that doesn't exist (like the 100th letter of a short word), Python will complain with an error!

quiz.question: What happens if we try to change a single letter in a text using its index (e.g. text[0] = 'a')?
options: The lyrics are changed without any problems.
The lyrics will stop at the end of the text.
Python scolds and reports an error, because texts cannot be changed after they are created (they are immutable).

sections.content:
Imagine that a word is like a train, and each letter travels in a numbered carriage. In Python, the first letter is in box zero (`0`)! To get a letter, we put the carriage number in square brackets (ex: `texto[0]`). If we want to count backwards, we use negative numbers (the `-1` is always the last car).

You can also take entire 'chunks' of the train using **slicing**. Just put `[start:end]`. It will pick up the letters from the beginning and stop just before the end.
sections.example:
word = 'Python'
print(word[0])   # 'P'
print(word[-1])  # 'n' (last)

# Slicing
print(word[0:2]) # 'Py'
print(word[2:5]) # 'tho'
print(word[:2])  # 'Py' (omits start, assumes 0)
print(word[4:])  # 'on' (omits end, assumes the rest)

sections.content: String slicing can go even further by using a third parameter called 'step'. The full syntax is `text[start:end:step]`. If you use a negative step, for example `-1`, Python will read the text backwards, magically reversing the word!
sections.example:

# Skipping by 2 letters
print(text[0:6:2])  # Prints: Pto

# Quickly reversing a string
print(text[::-1])   # Prints: nohtyP

sections.content:
Remember we said that texts are plastered? **Lists**, on the other hand, are completely malleable (changeable)! They are created using square brackets `[]` and separating items with commas.

You can use the same 'train car' tricks (indexes and slicing) on ​​lists. The big difference is that, in a list, you can go there and change the content of a position, add new items or remove things at will, without having to create the whole list from scratch again.

lessons.title: Lesson 26: Multiple Assignment and While Loop
lessons.description: Learn the power of assigning values ​​to multiple things at once and repeating actions with the while loop.
tips: The print() function always skips to the next line at the end. If you want to avoid this, put `end=' '` inside it.

quiz.question: How does Python know which lines of code are part of the repeater (while loop) and which are outside it?

It guesses by itself if the code is short.

sections.content:
In Python, you can be agile and store several values ​​at the same time in a single line (ex: `age, weight = 25, 70`). This is called **multiple assignment**.

Another super power is the `while` loop (which means 'while'). It repeats a block of commands without stopping, *as long as* a condition is true. 

**Critical Warning:** Python is super annoying with tidying up (indentation). For it to know what is inside the `while` block, you **need** to put spaces (or Tab) before the lines, pushing the text to the right. If you don't align it correctly, it won't run!

a, b = 0, 1
while a < 10:
    print(a, end=' ')
    a, b = b, a + b
# Output: 0 1 1 2 3 5 8

Also, in the `while` loop, be extra careful with 'infinite loops': if you forget to update the control variable within the block, the loop will run forever.

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Flow Tools - If, For and Range
lessons.description: Learn how to make the computer make decisions with if and repeat with for and range.

options: The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 (it always starts from 0 and stops one number before).
An error warning that numbers are missing.

sections.content:
To make the program make decisions like a human, we use `if` (if). It's like the doorman at a nightclub: 'If you're over 18, come in'. If not, you can add `elif` (if it isn't, but is a friend of the owner, it goes in) or `else` (if it isn't any of that, it stays out).

Another fantastic tool is `for`. It allows you to 'take a look' at each item in a box (like a list) one by one. And if you just want to count numbers (e.g. count from 0 to 10), Python has `range()`, which is a super automatic generator of numerical sequences!

lessons.title: Lesson 28: Break, Continue and Else Clauses in Loops
lessons.description: Learn how to eject from a repeating loop or skip your turn.
tips: The 'pass' command is just a ghost. It does nothing, it just fills a space when Python forces you to write something.
The 'else' of a for/while loop is almost like a 'Phew, I finished everything without being interrupted!' message.

references.label: Break, Continue and Else in loops

quiz.question: When does the magic word 'else' stuck at the end of a 'for' loop actually run its internal code?
options: Every time we press the eject button (break).
Only the first time the loop rotates.
Only when the loop finishes its entire count and ends naturally (without taking a break).
Whenever the loop skips the turn (continue).

sections.content:
Imagine that you are running a loop (`for` or `while`) looking for your lost keys. If you found the keys early on, you don't need to keep looking, right? This is where the `break` comes in: he presses the 'eject button' and ends the repetition immediately!

`Continue` is like 'skipping your turn' in a board game: it ignores the rest of that cycle and skips straight to the next repetition.

And a crazy Python fact: you can put an `else` at the end of a loop! This `else` is only triggered if you finished the entire repetition naturally, WITHOUT using the `break` button.

exercises.description: 1. Write a `for i in range(5):` loop and use the `break` command if `i == 2` to break the loop. Print the value of `i` every cycle before the break.
2. Create a loop `for i in range(4):` where if `i == 1` you use `continue`. Print the remaining numbers.
3. Write a `for i in range(2):` loop that prints 'Ok' in the block and has an `else` clause printing 'End'.
4. Use a `while True:` to print 'Rodou' and then give a `break`.
5. In a `for i in range(5):` loop, if `i` is even (i % 2 == 0), apply a `continue`. Print the remainder (the odd numbers).

sections.content: Although `break` is an excellent escape route, it is recommended to keep using `break` and `continue` with caution so as not to make the flow of your code too confusing (the famous 'spaghetti code'). `else` coupled with `for` is perfect for 'search' situations, where if we don't find anything (without break), we execute a standard action at the end.

exercises.description: 6. Make a `while i < 3` loop with an `else` that prints 'Finished'. Print `i` inside the while (start `i = 1`).
7. In a `for` iterating over `[10, 20, 30]`, use `break` after printing the 10.
8. Iterating over `[1, 2, 3]`, use `continue` on number 2. Print the rest.
9. Make a loop with unconditional `break` on the first repetition `for i in range(2):`. Print 'Break' before leaving.
10. Use `pass` inside a `for i in range(1):` loop followed by an `else` that prints 'Done'.

lessons.title: Class 24: Match Instruction and Definition of Functions
lessons.description: Discover how to create your own magical tools (functions).
tips: Always use obvious names for your functions (e.g., calculate_age). This makes it easy to remember what they do.
The 'case _' in match is like the 'None of the above' option in a test.

quiz.question: In Python's multiple choice panel (the match), what is the drawer with the underscore (case _) for?
options: To cause a mistake on purpose.
It is the 'wildcard' case that will act as the default if none of the previous options work.

sections.content:
`match` works like a super multiple choice panel. You give it a value, and it tests drawer by drawer (`case`) to see which one fits. If it doesn't fit in any of them, the wildcard drawer `case _` (with an underscore) solves the problem.

And if you made really cool code and don't want to keep copying and pasting it all the time, you can package it using the word `def`. By doing this, you have just invented a **Function**: a brand new tool, with a name of its own, ready to be used as many times as you want in the program!
sections.example:
def respond_status(status):
    """Returns a simple description based on HTTP status code."""
    match status:
        case 400:
            return "Bad request"
        case 404:
            return "Not found"
        case _:
            return "Something went wrong"

print(respond_status(404))

exercises.description: 1. Define a simple function called `welcome()` that takes no parameters and just returns the string 'Hello, World!'. Then call it and display the result.
2. Define a function `double(n)` that returns twice a number. Print the result of `double(5)`.
3. Create a `match` structure for the variable `opcao = 2`. In `case 1:` print 'One', in `case 2:` print 'Two'.
4. Use a `match` with the variable `command = 'skip'`. If you don't find any matching `case`, use `case _:` to print 'Unknown command'.
5. Define a function `sum(a, b)` that returns the sum. Print `add(4, 6)`.

sections.content: `match-case` (introduced in Python 3.10) doesn't just do simple checks, it supports advanced patterns like capturing variables and checking data types at the same time! It is infinitely more powerful than a simple switch-case in other languages. And for functions, remember that they allow you to return multiple values ​​at once, thanks to the magic of tuples.
sections.example:
# Returning multiple values
def min_max(a, b):
    return min(a,b), max(a,b)

smallest, largest = min_max(10, 5)
print(smallest, largest)  # Prints: 5 10

# Match with capture (Advanced example)
command = ['move', 'left']
match command:
    case ['move', direction]:
        print('Moving to', direction)

exercises.description: 6. Define a function `greet(name)` that prints the welcome message, e.g. 'Hello Ana'. Call with 'Joao'.
7. Make a `match` for the value `status = 404`. Use the wildcard to print 'Error' if it is any value other than 200.
8. Create a function called `eh_par(n)` that returns 'Yes' if n % 2 == 0 and 'No' if not. Print `eh_par(4)`.
9. Make an empty function `def nada():` using `pass` in the body. Call it and print 'Ready'.
10. Use `match` to evaluate `fruit = 'maca'`. If it is 'stretcher' print 'Red', if 'banana' print 'Yellow'.

lessons.title: Class 25: Tuples - Immutable Collections
lessons.description: Learn about tuples in Python, how to create them, unpack them, and why immutability is useful.
lessons.content:
### What are Tuples?

A **Tuple** is an ordered sequence of elements, very similar to a List, but with a fundamental difference: **tuples are immutable**! This means that once it is created, you cannot add, remove, or modify elements of a tuple.

**Syntax:**
```python
point = (10, 20)
colors = ('red', 'green', 'blue')
```

**Advantages of Tuples:**
- **Performance**: They are lighter and faster than lists in memory.
- **Data security**: Ensures that fixed data (e.g. GPS coordinates, settings) will not be changed by accident.
- **Unwrapping**: It's easy to assign values from a tuple directly to variables:
```python
x, y = point
print(x) # 10
```
lessons.example:
# Creating and unpacking tuples
point = (100, 200)
x, y = point
print(f'X={x}, Y={y}')

# Attempting to change raises TypeError:
# point[0] = 50  # Error!

exercises.description: 1. Create a tuple called `coordinates` with the values ​​`(5, 10)`. Print the first element using index 0.
2. Create a tuple `data = ('Ana', 25)`. Unpack it into the variables `name` and `age`, and then print the variable `name`.

tips: Use parentheses () to define tuples.
To create a tuple of just 1 element, put a comma at the end: `unit = (5,)`.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between a List and a Tuple in Python?
options: Tuples only accept numbers, while lists accept any data type
Tuples are immutable, while lists can be modified
Lists use parentheses and tuples use square brackets
There is no difference, both are exactly the same

lessons.title: Class 26: Dictionaries - Mapping Keys and Values
lessons.description: Master the dictionary structure in Python to associate unique keys with values.
lessons.content:
### What are Dictionaries?

A **Dictionary** (`dict`) is a mutable collection of **key:value** pairs. While lists use numeric indexes (0, 1, 2...), dictionaries use text keys or numbers to find information instantly.

**Syntax:**
```python
student = {
    'name': 'Carlos',
    'age': 22,
    'course': 'Python'
}
```

**Main Operations:**
- **Access value**: `aluno['nome']` or `aluno.get('nome')` 
- **Add/Update**: `aluno['grade'] = 9.5` 
- **Iterate**: `.keys()`, `.values()`, `.items()`
lessons.example:
student = {'name': 'Beatriz', 'grade': 10}
print(student['name'])

# Adding a new key
student['course'] = 'Engineering'
print(student['course'])

exercises.description: 1. Create a dictionary `product = {'name': 'Keyboard', 'price': 150}`. Print the value associated with the `'name'` key.
2. Create a dictionary `car = {'brand': 'Ford'}`. Add the key `'year'` with the value `2020` and print `car['year']`.

tips: Dictionary keys must be unique and immutable (strings and numbers are ideal).
The `.get('key', default)` method prevents the program from crashing if the key doesn't exist.

quiz.question: How do we access the value associated with the 'age' key in a dictionary called `person`?

lessons.title: Class 27: Sets - Single Elements
lessons.description: Discover how to use sets in Python to eliminate duplicate elements and perform mathematical operations.
lessons.content:
### What are Sets?

A **Set** is an unordered collection of **unique** elements. It is perfect for removing duplicate items from a collection and performing mathematical operations such as Union, Intersection and Difference.

**Syntax:**
```python
numbers = {1, 2, 3, 3, 3}
print(numbers) # Prints: {1, 2, 3}
```

**Methods and Operations:**
- `add(item)`: Adds an element.
- `remove(item)`: Removes an element.
- **Union (`|`)**: Combines two sets.
- **Intersection (`&`)**: Returns only the elements present in both sets.
lessons.example:
# Removing duplicates from a list
list_with_duplicates = [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4]
unique_set = set(list_with_duplicates)
print(sorted(list(unique_set)))  # Prints: [1, 2, 3, 4]

exercises.description: 1. Create a list `nums = [1, 1, 2, 3, 3]`. Convert to `set`, then find the size using `len()` and print.
2. Create a set `fruits = {'maca', 'banana'}`. Add `'orange'` with `.add()` and print if `'orange' in fruits`.

tips: Sets do not have indices, so you cannot do `my_set[0]`.
To create an empty set use `set()`, because `{}` creates an empty dictionary.

quiz.question: What happens when adding a duplicate element to a `set` in Python?
options: The element is ignored and the set remains with just one copy of it
The element replaces the previous element
The set accepts and duplicates the information

lessons.title: Class 28: Delving deeper into Functions (Parameters, Returns and Scope)
lessons.description: Learn how to create professional functions with return values, default parameters, and scope control.
lessons.content:
### Mastering Functions in Python

Functions are the fundamental blocks for organizing reusable code. In this class, we will advance in the study of **return values** with `return`, **default parameters** and **scope of variables**.

**The `return` command:**
A function that does not use `return` returns `None`. `return` returns the result to whoever called the function and ends its execution immediately.

```python
def multiply(a, b):
    return a * b

result = multiply(3, 4)
print(result) # 12
```

**Standard Parameters:**
```python
def greet(name="Student"):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
```

exercises.description: 1. Define a function `double(n)` that returns twice as much as n. Print `double(5)`.
2. Create a function `saudacao(nome='Aluno')` that returns `'Hello ' + name`. Print `greeting()`.

tips: Avoid using global variables inside functions; pass values as parameters.
You can return multiple values by separating them with commas (Python will automatically create a Tuple).

quiz.question: What happens if a function does not have a `return` statement?
options: It runs in an infinite loop

lessons.title: Class 29: Native Modules and Libraries (math, random, datetime)
lessons.description: Learn how to import and reuse the native modules provided in the Python standard library.
lessons.content:
### What are Modules?

A **Module** is a file containing ready-to-use Python definitions and commands. Python already comes with the so-called "included battery" (Standard Library) full of useful modules!

**Importing Modules:**
```python
import math
print(math.sqrt(16)) # Square root -> 4.0

import random
drawn_number = random.randint(1, 10)
```

**Import Syntax:**
- `import module`: Imports the complete module.
- `from modulo import funcao`: Imports only the specific function.
lessons.example:
import math
from random import choice

print(math.ceil(4.2))  # Rounds up -> 5
fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'grape']
print(choice(fruits) in fruits)  # Prints True

exercises.description: 1. Import the `math` module. Print the value of the rounded Pi constant with `round(math.pi, 2)`.
2. Import the `random` module. Use `random.randint(5, 5)` to generate a number in the range [5, 5] and print it.

tips: Use `import math` for trigonometric operations, logarithms, and roots.
Always insert `import` commands at the beginning of your code file.

quiz.question: Which keyword is used to include the functionality of a native module in your Python code?

lessons.title: Lesson 35: Error Handling (try, except, finally)
lessons.description: Learn how to handle exceptions and errors at runtime to prevent your application from breaking.
lessons.content:
### Exception Handling in Python

Mistakes happen! For example, when the user tries to divide a number by zero or types text where we expected a number. Instead of allowing the application to break, we use `try-except` blocks.

**Basic Structure:**
```python
try:
    number = int("abc")
except ValueError:
    print("Error: Invalid entry!")
finally:
    print("Execution completed.")
```

**Types of Common Exceptions:**
- `ValueError`: Incompatible value.
- `ZeroDivisionError`: Division by zero.
- `TypeError`: Incorrect data type.

exercises.description: 1. Write a `try` block that divides 10 by 0. Catch the `ZeroDivisionError` exception and print 'No division by zero'.
exercises.expected_output: You shall not divide by zero

exercises.description: 2. Create a `try` block trying to convert the `'python'` string to an integer with `int()`. Catch `ValueError` and print 'Invalid text'.

tips: Avoid catching generic exceptions (`except:` without a specific type); catch specific errors.
The `finally` block always executes, whether an error occurs or not (ideal for closing files or connections).

references.label: Official Python Documentation - Errors and Exceptions

quiz.question: Which block of code is ALWAYS executed, regardless of whether an exception occurred or not?

lessons.title: Class 31: File Manipulation (open, read, write)
lessons.description: Learn how to read and write persistent text files to disk with Python.
lessons.content:
### Manipulating Files in Python

To save data permanently to disk, we use the `open()` function. The best practice in Python is to use the `with` context manager, which guarantees automatic closing of the file.

**Opening Modes:**
- `'w'`: Writing (overwrites the file).
- `'a'`: Attachment (adds to the end of the file).
- `'r'`: Reading.

```python
# Writing to a file
with open('nota.txt', 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('Hello, file!')

# Reading from file
with open('nota.txt', 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    content = f.read()
    print(content)
```
lessons.example:
import tempfile
import os

# Creating a temporary file for testing
path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), 'test.txt')
with open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    f.write('Line 1')

with open(path, 'r', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    print(f.read())

exercises.description: 1. Open a file using `with open('dados_teste.txt', 'w') as f:` and write the string 'Pyeduc'. Then open it in `'r'` mode and print the content.
2. Create a file `teste_a.txt` with 'A'. Open in `'a'` mode, write 'B'. Open in `'r'` mode and print the content.

tips: Always use `encoding='utf-8'` when working with text files to avoid accentuation issues.
The `with` context manager closes the file automatically even if an error occurs during reading/writing.

references.label: Official Python Documentation - Reading and Writing Files

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of using the `with open(...)` block when manipulating files?
options: Guarantees that the file will be closed automatically when leaving the block
Prevents the file from being deleted from the computer

lessons.title: Class 32: Introduction to Object Orientation (Classes and Objects)
lessons.description: Understand the fundamentals of the Object Orientation paradigm in Python.
lessons.content:
### What is Object Orientation (OOP)?

OOP is a programming paradigm that organizes code around **Objects** (representations of the real world) created from **Classes** (templates or projects).

**Key Concepts:**
- **Class**: The template (`class Pessoa:`).
- **Object**: The instance created from the class (`p1 = Pessoa()`).
- `__init__`: The constructor method invoked when creating the object.
- `self`: Reference to the object instance itself.

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def present(self):
        return f"Hello, my name is {self.name}!"
```

exercises.description: 1. Create a `Book` class with `__init__(self, title)`. Instantiate with `'Python 101'` and print the `.title` attribute.
2. Create a `Calculator` class with the `add(self, a, b)` method that returns `a + b`. Instantiate `calc = Calculadora()` and print `calc.sum(3, 7)`.

tips: By convention in Python, Class names use CamelCase (e.g., `BankAccount`).
The first parameter of any instance method inside a class MUST be `self`.

quiz.question: What is the function of the `self` parameter in class methods in Python?
options: Identifies that the method is static and global
Refers to the current instance of the object executing the method
It is an optional parameter reserved for the operating system
Convert the class to a dictionary
